opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest test is this: is the robot doing a real job, for a real customer, every day, without a team of engineers standing behind it? A lot of what we see in this industry is demonstrations. You film a robot folding a shirt or making coffee, maybe it took fifty tries, maybe someone is teleoperating it off camera, and it goes viral. That tells you something about the potential of the technology, but it tells you almost nothing about productivity.

So when I look at a company, including my own, I ask a few concrete questions.

First, is there a paying customer who would be upset if you took the robot away? Not a pilot or a strategic showcase, but someone who has built the robot into their operations, in a pharmacy, a warehouse, a factory line, and would have to hire people back if it disappeared. That's the strongest signal.

Second, look at the operating numbers, not the peak performance. How many hours a day does it run? What's the success rate over thousands of attempts, not the best clip? How often does a human have to step in, and how long does recovery take? A robot that succeeds 95% of the time can still be useless if each failure stops the line for twenty minutes. Productivity lives in the long tail of failures.

Third, the economics per unit. What does the hardware cost, what does deployment cost, how long until the customer gets their money back? If every new site needs months of custom engineering, collecting data, retuning, then you have a services business that happens to involve robots. Real productivity means the second, tenth and hundredth deployment get dramatically cheaper and faster, because the model generalizes across environments and objects.

And fourth, honesty about autonomy. I'd ask directly: what fraction of the task is truly autonomous? Teleoperation is a legitimate tool for data collection, but if it's quietly carrying the product, the business won't scale.

That's why at Galbot we focused early on specific scenarios, like retail and pharmacy picking, where the task is well defined, the value is clear, and we can deploy at scale and learn from real data, rather than chasing a general-purpose robot that only works on stage. Embodied intelligence will become general eventually, but the path there is through real deployments that actually pay for themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says to look for a real job and customer, and notes that demonstrations may be teleoperated. It does not propose a public demonstration without teleoperation as the first test.

r002.rationale: It asks how many hours a robot runs and discusses factory lines, but does not identify the amount of work robots actually perform each day in a factory as evidence.

r003.rationale: It recommends examining operating numbers across thousands of attempts, but does not call for long-term operational reporting.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes paying customers from pilots and strategic showcases, but does not say strategic agreement announcements are becoming less persuasive evidence of productivity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest test is this: is the robot doing work that someone would otherwise have to pay a person to do, in a real environment, for a long enough stretch that the customer keeps paying for it? If the answer to all three parts is yes, you're delivering productivity. If any part is missing, you're probably still doing demos.

Let me unpack that, because the industry is very good at making demos look like deployment.

First, "real environment." A robot that works beautifully in our lab in Beijing, with our lighting, our shelves, our objects placed by our own engineers, is not the same as a robot in a pharmacy at two in the morning with a box someone left in the wrong place and a shelf that's slightly tilted. The gap between those two is where most of the engineering actually lives. When I look at a company, I want to know how many sites they are running in that they do not control. Not how many sites they have visited, not how many pilots they have signed, but how many locations have the robot running without a company engineer standing next to it.

Second, duration and intervention rate. A lot of people quote success rates, ninety-five percent, ninety-eight percent, whatever. I care more about how many times per day a human has to step in, and what it costs when they do. If a robot picks correctly ninety-eight times out of a hundred but the two failures stop the whole line and someone has to drive over, you have not replaced a worker, you've added a very expensive new worker who needs a babysitter. The honest metric is hours of unattended operation and the cost per intervention. Companies that are really delivering value will tell you those numbers, because they're proud of them. Companies that aren't will change the subject to the model architecture.

Third, and this is the one investors sometimes forget, the customer has to keep paying. Not a one-time purchase funded by an innovation budget. Recurring payment, renewals, expansion to more stores or more lines. A customer renewing is a much more honest signal than any benchmark, because the customer doesn't care about your foundation model, they care whether their labor cost went down or their throughput went up. When we started with pharmacies, we were very clear that the pharmacy chain was not going to pay us for being cute. They would pay us if the robot could handle night shifts and reduce their staffing. That forced us to be honest with ourselves.

There are also a few things that I think are false signals, or at least weak ones. Humanoid form factor by itself tells you nothing about productivity. The number of degrees of freedom tells you nothing. A video of a robot folding a shirt tells you nothing unless you know how many takes it took. Even a very large amount of training data is only meaningful if it transfers to the environments where the robot is actually being paid to work. We spend an enormous amount of effort on simulation and synthetic data precisely because we want generalization to the messy, unseen case, and the only real proof of that is deployment numbers.

So if I had to give one practical question for anyone evaluating a robotics company, it's this: ask them what percentage of their revenue comes from robots that are doing work right now, today, with no company employee on site, and ask what the customer's cost per task is compared to a human. If they can answer that without hesitation, they are on the productivity side of the line. If they start talking about the future of embodied intelligence instead, they are still on the demo side. There's nothing wrong with being on the demo side, we all start there, but you should know which one you're looking at.

r001.rationale: The response’s first test is whether a robot does paid work in a real environment over time. It does not propose a public demonstration without teleoperation.

r002.rationale: It discusses unattended hours, interventions, and customer cost per task, but does not identify the amount of work robots perform each day in a factory.

r003.rationale: It calls for sustained operating evidence, including unattended-operation hours and intervention costs, and says companies should disclose those metrics so productivity can be assessed.

r004.rationale: It says signed pilots are not evidence of running deployments and that customer renewals are a more honest signal, making agreement announcements less persuasive than ongoing paid operation.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with the task the customer needs done. Can the robot do it reliably, and does it reduce the total cost of getting that work done? A robot performing an impressive demo is one thing; a robot working every day at a customer’s site is another.

You have to count the whole system: installation, maintenance, downtime, and how often a person has to step in. If you save one operator’s time but need another person constantly supervising the robot, the productivity gain may be very small.

So I’d look at actual operating results: output per hour, quality, cost per completed task, and the time it takes the customer to recover their investment. And I’d ask whether customers expand deployment after the initial trial. When a customer sees enough value to buy more robots and use them in daily operations, that’s a much stronger signal than a compelling demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts impressive demos with daily customer-site performance, but does not propose a public demonstration without teleoperation as the first test.

r002.rationale: It mentions output per hour and daily operations, but does not identify how much work robots perform each day in a factory.

r003.rationale: It calls for assessing actual operating results, but does not call for long-term operational reporting.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss strategic agreement announcements or their value as evidence of productivity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to look at what happens after the demo. Can the robot do useful work reliably, day after day, in a real customer’s operation? And does the customer get more output for the total cost?

That cost includes more than the robot. You have integration, maintenance, downtime, and the people needed to supervise it or recover from failures. If you automate a task but create an equally expensive support burden, the productivity gain may disappear.

So I would look at sustained performance in deployment, how much human intervention is required, and whether customers expand their use after seeing the economics. A customer buying more because the first deployment paid for itself is a much stronger signal than an impressive demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response says to look beyond a demo, but does not propose a public demonstration or specify that it should be without teleoperation.

r002.rationale: It discusses useful work and sustained performance, but does not identify the amount of work robots perform each day in a factory.

r003.rationale: It calls for sustained performance in deployment, but does not call for long-term operational reporting.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss strategic agreement announcements or their persuasiveness as evidence of productivity.
